narrativeReportMd:
# HumanName R4-to-R6 breaking-change assessment

## Bottom line
No local hard instance-breaking HumanName content-model changes were found. R4 instances using the existing HumanName fields remain structurally valid against the R6 datatype shape.

## Scope
I compared the R4 and R6 core `StructureDefinition/HumanName` artifacts, package identity metadata, package index entries, and the directly bound `NameUse` ValueSet/CodeSystem. Inherited `Element`, `DataType`, and `Extension` changes are explicitly out of scope.

## Main migration themes
The element set, cardinalities, primitive/datatype choices, modifier flags, summary flags, order meanings, and required name-use code set are stable. The only local notable change is semantic text at the root: R6 describes HumanName as normally human but also usable for other living entities, while R4 described it as a human's name.

## Highest-impact findings
No Critical or High local findings were identified. The root semantic widening is Low impact: it does not reject R4 data, but it can matter to applications or mappings that treat `HumanName` as intrinsically person-only.

## Findings requiring human review
No local finding requires human review for schema migration. Human review may still be useful for organizations with business rules that prohibit non-human subjects from using `HumanName`.

## Backward-compatible design observations
The R6 change appears to clarify and widen the datatype's intended domain without changing the wire format. A less disruptive alternative would have been usage-site narrative or profiles, but that would leave the reusable datatype less explicit.

## Follow-up analysis
The R4-to-R6 base-definition change from `Element` to `DataType` should be handled by the `DataType` or base infrastructure report, not by this HumanName report.

summary.executiveSummaryMd: No local hard instance-breaking changes were found for `HumanName`. The stable content model means existing R4 name data should validate structurally in R6; the main migration note is the R6 semantic widening to other living entities. The main uncertainty is lack of an official diff or narrative change note explaining the intent.
summary.migrationThemesMd: Migration is mostly a no-op for persisted data and generated element properties. Code generators should continue to expose the same local fields. Validation suites should still include the `use` required-binding enum and ensure modifier handling for `use` remains unchanged. Business rules that assumed `HumanName` always means a human person's name should be reviewed before accepting R6 non-human living-entity use cases.
summary.confidenceSummaryMd: Confidence is high for the local structural comparison because both core StructureDefinitions and directly bound local terminology artifacts were available and computably compared. Confidence is lower for the policy rationale behind the root text change because no official diff or narrative change note was supplied.

findings.title: Root definition widens HumanName from a human's name to a name normally of a human or other living entity

oldState.summary: R4 described HumanName as a human's name with parts and usage.

semanticText.short: Name of a human - parts and usage
semanticText.definition: A human's name with the ability to identify parts and usage.
semanticText.comment: Names may be changed, or repudiated, or people may have different names in different contexts. Names may be divided into parts of different type that have variable significance depending on context, though the division into parts does not always matter. With personal names, the different parts might or might not be imbued with some implicit meaning; various cultures associate different importance with the name parts and the degree to which systems must care about name parts around the world varies widely.

newState.summary: R6 describes HumanName as normally human but usable for other living entities assigned names by a human, excluding organizations.

semanticText.definition: A name, normally of a human, that can be used for other living entities (e.g. animals but not organizations) that have been assigned names by a human and may need the use of name parts or the need for usage information.

structuredDelta.matchingRationaleMd: The same canonical StructureDefinition, id, type, and root element id are present in both packages; only the root descriptive text changed.

impact.impactRationaleMd: This is not a schema or validator break for existing R4 instances: no element was added, removed, made mandatory, narrowed, or retyped. The risk is semantic. R6-valid use of `HumanName` for an animal or other non-organization living entity has the same JSON/XML shape, but it is not cleanly represented by the R4 definition's narrower human-only wording. Runtime impact is limited to code, mappings, or business rules that attach human-person semantics to the datatype name rather than to the resource or profile using it.
impact.safetyOrBusinessRiskMd: No direct patient-safety issue was identified from the datatype shape. The practical risk is misclassification or rejection in systems with person-only assumptions.

justification.inferredGoal: Clarify that the reusable name-parts datatype can describe named living entities beyond human persons while still excluding organizations.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeSummary: Not applicable: the R6 wording widens semantics without invalidating R4-valid HumanName instances.
justification.justificationRationaleMd: The inferred goal is reasonable: R6 clarifies that the same name-parts datatype can be used for other named living entities while still excluding organizations. The local element set, cardinalities, types, modifier flags, and required NameUse codes remain stable, so this is not an R4-to-R6 instance-breaking design change. Because no official change note was supplied, the rationale is inferred rather than confirmed, so `Probably justified` is more appropriate than an unqualified `Justified` verdict.
justification.backwardCompatibleAlternativeMd: Backward-compatible alternative analysis is not applicable in the breaking-change sense because existing R4 `HumanName` data remains representable and valid under the R6 shape. R6 could have kept the older human-only root wording and documented animal or other living-entity usage only at resource/profile sites, but that would be an alternative semantic-documentation choice, not a base-design alternative needed to preserve R4 instances. Its main tradeoff would be weaker and less discoverable cross-artifact guidance.
justification.alternativeTradeoffSummary: No less-breaking base design is needed for R4 preservation; leaving the R4 wording unchanged would avoid semantic surprise but would not express the reusable datatype's R6 scope.

examples.examplesMd: A concrete JSON fragment is not shown because the semantic difference is about the named entity outside the `HumanName` value itself. The same `{ "text": "Fluffy" }` fragment could be syntactically valid in both versions; the difference is whether the surrounding use asserts a non-human living entity that R6 now explicitly permits.

findings.narrativeMd: `HumanName` keeps the same wire representation but its root conformance text is broader in R6. Existing R4 data does not become invalid. The migration concern is for implementations that treated the datatype itself as proof that the subject is a human person, or that reject names for animals or other living entities because the R4 definition was human-only.
findings.validationAndCompatibilityMd: There is no old-valid/new-invalid mechanism here: the local element set and cardinalities are unchanged. R6-to-R4 is semantically lossy for non-human living-entity use cases because R4 can carry the same fields but its definition does not clearly authorize that use. Strict generated schemas and enum switches should not break from this change alone.
findings.migrationGuidanceMd: No data transform is needed for ordinary R4 person names. Review domain validation, terminology mappings, UI labels, and documentation that equate `HumanName` with a human patient/person name. For backward conversion, preserve the name fields but consider profile-specific notes or extensions if the fact that the name belongs to a non-human living entity must be retained.
findings.backwardCompatibilityAnalysisMd: The change was probably avoidable in the narrow sense that R6 could have preserved the R4 wording and documented non-human usage elsewhere. However, because no wire-format or validation rule changed, the selected approach is already relatively backward-compatible; its tradeoff is semantic surprise rather than instance rejection.
findings.reviewerNotesMd: The analysis did not find a local structural break. If downstream reports identify resources that newly use `HumanName` for animals or other entities, those resource-specific changes should be evaluated in those artifacts.

freshReview.narrativeMd: R6 changes the root `HumanName` description from a strictly human name to a name normally of a human that can also be used for other living entities such as animals, while still excluding organizations. At the path level this is a semantic widening: the datatype's children, cardinalities, required `use` binding strength, summary/modifier behavior, and wire representation remain the same. Existing R4 instances using `HumanName` remain structurally valid in R6, and generated model APIs should not need property-shape changes for this finding. The only plausible migration concern is business logic that treated the datatype label itself as proof that the named subject is human; that is a policy assumption to review, not a base validation break.
keyEvidence: R4 StructureDefinition `HumanName` root short/definition: `Name of a human - parts and usage` / `A human's name with the ability to identify parts and usage.`

R6 StructureDefinition `HumanName` root short/definition: `Name of a human or other living entity - parts and usage` / `A name, normally of a human, that can be used for other living entities (e.g. animals but not organizations)...`

R4 and R6 `HumanName` element summaries show the same local child paths and cardinalities: `use`, `text`, `family`, `given`, `prefix`, `suffix`, and `period`; `use` remains 0..1 code with required NameUse binding and modifier=true.
R4 maturity/status evidence checked: supplied FMM is normative and the R4 StructureDefinition carries standards-status `normative` with normative-version `4.0.0`.
freshReview.fmmEffect: Normative R4 status raises the expected stability bar, so a narrowing, deletion, or hard validation change would need strong justification. Here the change is a semantic widening with preserved structure and therefore the normative status does not make it a material compatibility problem.
freshReview.compatibilityMechanism: semantic/documentation: the practical effect is changed conformance meaning at the root datatype description, not old-valid/new-invalid validation, runtime/API/codegen breakage, or R6-to-R4 data loss for the represented name fields.
freshReview.lessBreakingAlternativeAssessment: No less-breaking base R6 design is needed for compatibility because the existing R6 design already preserves the R4 wire shape and accepts existing R4 data. Keeping the old human-only wording would fail the apparent R6 goal of allowing names for other living entities, while introducing a separate parallel name datatype would add duplicate representations and codegen burden for little compatibility benefit.
freshReview.comparisonToExisting: agree: the existing report's low/no-material-breaking assessment is consistent with the independent review. It did not record an explicit less-breaking alternative judgment, and my fresh assessment is that an alternative is not applicable because there is no meaningful break to avoid.

checkedNoMaterialChange.notesMd: Canonical URL, id, name, kind, type, derivation, status, and abstract flag remain stable. The baseDefinition changes from `Element` to `DataType`, but that is an inherited/base hierarchy issue and not counted as a local HumanName finding.
Both snapshots contain the same local HumanName element paths: `use`, `text`, `family`, `given`, `prefix`, `suffix`, and `period`, plus inherited `id` and `extension`.
All matching local elements retain the same cardinalities: `use`, `text`, `family`, and `period` are `0..1`; `given`, `prefix`, and `suffix` are `0..*`; the root remains `0..*`.
Local element types are unchanged: `use` is `code`; `text`, `family`, `given`, `prefix`, and `suffix` are `string`; `period` is `Period`.
`HumanName` has no reference-typed local elements in either R4 or R6.

`HumanName.use` remains a required binding to `NameUse`. The ValueSet version changes from `4.0.1` to `6.0.0-ballot4`, but the local complete CodeSystems contain the same concepts: `usual`, `official`, `temp`, `nickname`, `anonymous`, `old`, and child code `maiden`.

No HumanName-specific invariant was added, removed, or strengthened. Differences in inherited `Element`/`Extension` constraints and XPath metadata are base-artifact issues and excluded from local findings.
No local fixed values, pattern values, or default values were found on HumanName elements in either version.
No local `maxLength`, regex, minValue, or maxValue limits were found on HumanName elements in either version.
`HumanName.use` remains `isModifier=true` with the same modifier reason. Other local elements remain non-modifier.
All local data-carrying HumanName elements retain `isSummary=true`; inherited `id` and `extension` remain `isSummary=false`.
No local HumanName slicing was introduced. The inherited open slicing on `extension` by `url` remains conceptually present but is treated as inherited Element/Extension behavior.
No local HumanName wire-format element names or choice-type representations changed. Runtime/codegen effects of the R6 `DataType` base class belong to the base datatype hierarchy analysis.

nonBreakingNotableChanges.title: HumanName root text now explicitly covers other living entities
nonBreakingNotableChanges.whyNotBreakingMd: The change widens descriptive semantics without changing the set of elements, cardinalities, types, flags, or required terminology codes. Existing R4 instances are not made invalid by the new wording.
nonBreakingNotableChanges.migrationAwarenessMd: Review code and documentation that treats the datatype name as implying a human person. The widened wording can affect R6-to-R4 policy decisions even though the serialized data remains compatible.

followUpDependencies.reasonMd: R6 `HumanName` specializes `DataType` whereas R4 specialized `Element`. Any generated-class inheritance, common datatype members, or base validation changes should be assessed in the `DataType`/base hierarchy report rather than duplicated here.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: No official R4-to-R6 diff or ballot rationale was available in the supplied inputs, so the intent behind the root semantic widening is inferred from the StructureDefinition text.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: An official HL7 change note, Jira ticket, or rendered R4/R6 diff explaining the HumanName wording change would confirm the rationale.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: A live terminology expansion was not performed. The local complete R4 and R6 `NameUse` CodeSystems and ValueSet compose definitions were compared instead and showed no code additions, removals, or definition changes.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Running a terminology server expansion for both `http://hl7.org/fhir/ValueSet/name-use|4.0.1` and `|6.0.0-ballot4` would independently confirm the computable comparison.

analysisLimitations.descriptionMd: The analysis used the StructureDefinition narrative embedded in the R6 JSON but did not inspect full rendered datatype pages or surrounding explanatory specification prose.
analysisLimitations.whatWouldResolveItMd: Reviewing the rendered R4 and R6 datatype pages could reveal additional non-computable notes about intended non-human usage or migration guidance.
